review:
I am 68 years old...and I love this game.  It is a real-time isometric strategy game that allows multiple ways to solve the puzzles to reach the end goal.  Been looking for a game like this for a long time.

The graphics are superb.  An elegantly designed environment.  A joy to just wander around in and explore.

I hope they add modules to keep this genre going.

If a soldier finds a body, they aren't just *more cautious for a few minutes before relaxing*, they sound the alarm.
If a soldier finds footprints they don't recognize in the snow, they make a beeline straight for the cover the footprints lead to.
If a soldier regularly sees another soldier, then suddenly finds post empty, they actually look around in nearby bushes.
If a soldier hears a sound meant to attract him, but it's up on a ledge, he's not going to climb up there.
This is a stealth game that takes the player seriously.

This is a rare game from an almost extinct genre. Clone of Commandos series from the 90s, but instead of world war setting, we got a feudal japan which is surprisingly works very well. The game mechanic is great too, if you played other games in the same genre such as Commandos, Desperados, or Robin Hood, you'll feel right at home. Usually I don't care much about the story, same like in Commandoes, but the story Shadow Tactics is more than decent, I enjoy it, and it has some twists as well.

The game is tough, but very satisfying. People say each mission needs 2-3 hours to complete, but I took 4-6 hours each mission because what I like about the genre is I can took my time, and feel the satisfaction of eliminating all enemies on map, stealthy..

I'm hoping for expansion, DLC, or sequel, but sadly the dev confirmed that there won't be any, but they're curently working on a new game but with a same genre.. and I can't wait to see it.

I guess all of us have games that we used to love back in the days, but can't find anything like them on modern market. Times changed and now there are many dead, or half-dead genres and sub-genres. Space simulators, rail shooters... Even real-time strategies and puzzle / point & click adventures aren't doing well now. Among all that there's a small [b]RTS[/b] sub-genre that was never really big, but still made a lot of loyal fans. I'm talking about [b]Commandos[/b] series and its clones. An unique mix of stealth and [b]RTS[/b] with revolutionary “cons of sight” system. By controlling group of soldiers with the unique set of abilities, players were supposed to finish different missions in [b]WWII[/b] setting. The first two [b]Commandos[/b] games (released in [b]1998[/b] and [b]2001[/b] respectively) were absolutely brilliant and it felt like their makers, [b]Pyro Studios[/b], are making instant classic. Unfortunately, the third [b]Commandos[/b] game wasn't that popular thanks to many questionable changes in the gameplay, while [b]FPS[/b] spin-off called [b]Commandos: Strike Force[/b] started the dark times for [b]Pyro Studios[/b]. Which switched to casual games soon after that. [b]Commandos[/b] series died. [i]But[/i] there was another team to keep their spirit alive.

In [b]2001[/b] (the same year with [b]Commandos 2[/b]) [b]German[/b] developer [b]Spellbound Entertainment[/b] released a game called [b]Desperados: Wanted Dead or Alive[/b]. And guess what? It was an exact copy of the first [b]Commandos[/b]. Just with more options and in [b]Wild West[/b] setting. Later, [b]Spellbound Entertainment[/b] will release two sequels to [b]Desperados[/b] and also two games of that kind in different settings. [b]Robin Hood: The Legend of Sherwood[/b] and [b]Chicago 1930[/b]. [b]Robin Hood: The Legend of Sherwood[/b] used to include advanced sword fights, while [b]Chicago 1930[/b] that was heavily inspired by [b]Brian De Palma[/b]'s cult movie [b]The Untouchables[/b], allowed us to play both as police and mafia. In other words, [b]Spellbound[/b] loved the genre and wanted to make more games in different settings. At some point they even planned a game called [b]Vampire Hunter[/b] in dark [b]Bram Stoker[/b]'s setting. A few screenshots exist, but unfortunately, the game itself was never released.

Why am I telling you all that? Well, because that's where the story of the entire sub-genre pretty much ends. After [b]Spellbound[/b] came to an end in [b]2012[/b], nobody really tried to make a proper game like that. Even ex-[b]Spellbound[/b] employees, who decided to stay in business and returned as [b]Black Forest Games[/b], showed no interest in such games. [b]Spellbound[/b] died and it looked like the spirit of [b]Commandos[/b] died with them. Until now. [b]Mimimi Productions[/b], another [b]German[/b] developer, came and... here we are. Meet [b]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/b]! The first proper [b]Commandos[/b] clone since forever.

And I must say, it's a [i]huge[/i] success. Mostly because [b]Mimimi Productions[/b] didn't try to alter the formula much. [b]Spellbound[/b]'s worst game of the kind was probably [b]Chicago 1930[/b]. Just because they tried too many different things at the same time. While the worst [b]Commandos[/b] was the third one. For the same exact reason. Too many new ideas that didn't really work out. The original formula was so good that there was literally no need for anything else. And [b]Mimimi[/b] understood that. Aside from the fact that [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] is a fully [b]3D[/b] game (the concept was polished enough before in [b]Desperados 2[/b] and [b]Helldorado[/b] and now it feels good and comfortable like never before), it's [i]the[/i] [b]Commandos[/b] that we all know and love. Actually, [b]Mimimi[/b] copied everything so well that most of your old skills from [b]Commandos[/b] and [b]Desperados[/b] will work here as well. It's like playing them all over again, really.

Of course, setting this time will be different. In [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] we have [b]Edo[/b] jidai [b]Japan[/b] ([b]1603[/b] – [b]1868[/b]) and a story about [b]Shōgun[/b] and the mysterious rebel leader [b]Kage[/b]-sama. But aside from that, there's pretty much no differences. Actually, even plot feels a lot like story from the very first [b]Desperados[/b]. I mean, [b]El Diablo[/b], [b]Kage-sama[/b]... you've got the idea. As for the characters and their abilities... those may look different, but technically, it's the same thing all over again. Like tanuki [b]Kuma[/b] will play a role of [b]Jack O'Hara[/b]'s radio, shurikens feel exactly like [b]James Blackwood[/b]'s throwing knives, a character called [b]Aiko[/b] is pretty much the same with [b]Natasha Nikochevski[/b] from expansion to the first [b]Comamndos[/b], etc.

In other words, [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] is like [b]Commandos[/b] in feudal [b]Japan[/b] setting. Or [b]Desperados[/b], because [b]Mimimi[/b] kept the best thing about the first [b]Desperados[/b] – the ability to give orders to the characters beforehand to perform at the same exact time. Remember [b]Quick Action[/b] from [b]Desperados[/b]? [b]Shadow Mode[/b] from [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] is exactly the same thing.

All that is kinda fun. Because usually when the game tries to copy another one so much, it's a bad thing. Usually, nobody likes clones. But this time... this time it's different. First of all, we didn't see anything like that for [i]ages[/i]. Second, in such games you don't really want anything new. You just want more. More missions. More, more and more. And [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] provides exactly that. Finally, it's a really well-made game. It looks very good for [b]Unity[/b] game, soundtrack is extremely charming and captures the mood very well, characters are very solid, while voices... Well, that's what I loved the most. Usually, when [b]English[/b]-speaking actors try to act like [b]Japanese[/b] people, it's a disaster. So, [b]Mimimi[/b] did an absolutely brilliant thing. They just hired [b]Japanese[/b] actors. Problem solved. Yep, this game has [b]Japanese[/b] voiceover. How cool is that? The answer is – [i]extremely[/i] cool. Personally, I think that every game with [b]Japanese[/b] characters should do exactly that. There's an [b]English[/b] voices too, though, in case if you want them. Everybody's happy.

So, in conclusion, [b]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/b] is a big comeback of [b]Commandos[/b]-like games. Extremely charming, extremely well-made and without any needless details. If you ever liked games from [b]Pyro[/b], or [b]Spellbound[/b], don't you even dare to miss the one from [b]Mimimi[/b]. The guys did [i]perfect[/i] job and the only thing I want to ask them... [i]Please, make a sequel!!![/i]

I use a Tobii eye tracking device for every day tasks because of my disability and I was very excited to find out that this game has an option to play it with it. It worked super well and I loved the game.

To give you context: I am more of a FPS guy, not really into RTS games. However, I had alot of fun playing this game.
You have 9 missions, but if you're new to the genre or to this game, each mission can take you 1.5 hours. They get more difficult, but even more satisfying to pull off. When you learn of a strategy you can use to take down three people without sounding an alarm, and even execute it beautifully, you will never get a feeling like that.

Honestly? Thanks to this, I am looking forward to more RTS stealth games like these, especially the upcoming Desperados III.

Personal Rating: 8 of 10

An excellent semi-hardcore real-time stealth tactical game. The game offers 5 different characters with distinguished abilities, skills and behaviour stratigically placed onto the map each level meaning you cannot choose who or how many to bring into each level. There are no leveling system, upgrades system or items to equipt. Each character and their skills are introduced pretty soon.

There are not many levels in the game and in my opinion it was just right. Each level is pre-generated meaning enemy locations and behaviour are fixed. If all these seem like a generic game so far, why the good rating?

First of all, since the game was set in Japan and it offers Japanese Language, naturally I choose that to feel more immersive and the voice acting is on point. It really feels like those of anime. Then the story; quite typical or predictable perhaps but be prepared to take your feelings on a roller coaster ride for the plot. This is because each character is so well designed that you can really feel attached to them. Speaking of immersive, the art style and design are just perfect to bring out the era and conditions of the game settings. The scores are well composed blend into the game perfectly too.

In addition to what is mentioned above, the game also does not offer much logic and surely you will notice when playing such as, bodies clipping through when stacked together or a small barrel can fit basically unlimited bodies. This has everything to do with the game design actually. The game focuses heavily on the stealth action part. Planning, exploring your options, taking opportunities, quick reaction, keen observation, making use of what is available and thinking outside the box are essential in this game and I literally mean all of those. You can feel the developers actually tested and played the game probably over and over again themselves to improve it to such extent with all the minor but great features. 

To name a few, you can pan the camera but at times you really need to be quick and so there is a toggle to allow you to highlight overlay interactable places. You can also place a pointer at any location and check for enemy vision on the specific point. Of course you can also select to view the enemy vision. There is also a simple mechanic for you to plan multiple actions for multiple characters and execute them with a push of a button.

Map designs, apart from being beautiful, are done so you can have multiple options or ways to tackle complete your goal. There are props or even event that you can create that could be a game changer. You just really need to use your imagination and do some trail and error. No big deal because the game also offers quick save and load at anytime.

Each mission allow plenty of time to think and play without punishing you. There are no rush mission (unless you want to take on the challenges) so you can have fun instead of pressure. Each mission has badges or challenges to complete. These are optional ofcourse but tackling them sometimes gives you more insight of what the game has to offer and the achievements well shows even more bizzare or imaginative methods to play.

Enemy A.I. are well crafted. They behave quite consistent and as predicted each time you replay so it really saves you the frustration of random events. The few enemy types are really something when they work together and can provide quite a challenge.

Overall, this is a pure stealth tactical that has simple yet refined mechanics and each of these mechanics and features complements each other perfectly like puzzle pieces.

Too good to be true in 2016:
- game is thrilling fun for many hours
- beautiful look
- nice English or Japanese voice-acting
- all texts are translated in many different languages
- superb soundtrack
- still works on small PCs, Macs and Linux-Systems without bugs
- offers you a demo where you can play 1.5 hours for free
- costs only under 40€ (a no-brainer or me after playing the demo on my Mac and PC)

Well, my late highlight in 2016 ! 
Good job, Mimimi and Daedalic!

Glorious resurrection of the long lost genre. Shadow Tactics Blades of the Shogun is everything a Commandos or Desperados fan could have asked for. It successfully captures the essence which made those games great & drastically improves it in every way. The world is vividly colorful, the animation is gorgeous to look at, the music & the voice over specially the Japanese one is really captivating & immersive which goes with the edo settings perfectly.

Gameplay wise it tests your patience a lot. Every level requires you to be really observant of the enemy's behavior as the A.I is smart & merciless. Coming up with genius of a plan to deal with a situation but ultimately seeing it unfolding as an utter failure when you execute the plan is one of the most agonizing moments in the game. It  happens, it will happen quite regularly but as soon as your carefully constructed plan meets the shiny colored perfection, that agony will turn into irresistible pleasure.

Also, the five playable characters, each of them with their own distinctive skillset are full of joys to play with. Their expressive banter during a mission makes u feel like they are alive rather than being just mundane.

In the end, people may regard Shadow Tactics as the spiritual successor of Commandos/Desperados but as a game it stands on its own with its unique charm. Its interestingly intriguing levels & the charming persona of the protagonists is  certainly a proof of that.
Also the game is finely polished. Runs butterly smooth on highest settings possible on my 2.5 years old rig! :)

This is the game I never knew I needed to play.

It brings back memories of playing the old Commando games.

The game is basically an isometric stealth game set in Edo-period Japan so most of the enemies you face will have guns. The first mission alone took me 1-2 hours to complete (that was from restarting it 5 times) so you'll probably get your money's worth once you finish the game.

Definitely a great game and I hope to see many more 'Shadow Tactics' games whether they be Japan or a different era. I'd love to see a Medieval England one.

The soundtrack is really nice comprising of traditional Japanese instruments. 
The voice acting is pretty good (at least the Japanese one). That's right, there's both English and Japanese voices to choose from. I have chosen Japanese voices due to authenticity.

The story of the game is mainly fictional. There's a few fictional outfits on certain NPC's for example. Guns tend to fire faster than they actually could. There's also no mention of the Tokugawa shogunate despite it being Edo themed. The story is purely made up, but that doesn't mean it's bad.

Overall, it's a great game. A nice little gem among all these early access games, anime visual novels and poorly made games.

The price is debatable in honesty, but I'm finding it worth what I paid so far.

P.S - Forgive me for any spelling errors.

This game is proof that a 97% positive rating doesn't mean the game is 97% good, but it is still an excellent experience well worth the playthrough.

Other reviewers have correctly pointed out that Shadow Tactics is essentially a puzzle game that happens to use stealth as a mechanic.  There are 13 levels, and in each, the objective is some variation of "Determine the correct order to kill enemies in order to get from point A to point B."  Sometimes the objective is to rescue someone, sometimes it's to kill someone, sometimes it's to steal something, but the end goal never affects the gameplay required to get there.

And that's unfortunate, because I grew tired of the gameplay long before I grew tired of the game (which never happened).  From any design perspective you choose, the game is outstanding.  The story is good, the environments are beautiful, the music is appropriate and sounds great, the five characters all have unique abilities that synergize wonderfully, and the voice talent is top notch (even though you can hear they're English actors trying to sound Japanese - or not even trying, in the case of Yuki).  Even the levels as puzzles are masterfully crafted.  The final level, in particular, is fiendishly designed, and I can't even imagine the hours of playtesting it took to get the enemy positioning and timing so perfect.

But, at the end of the day, Shadow Tactics IS just a repetitive puzzle solver - one I stuck with primarily because I liked the story and knew there weren't many levels.  The levels, played meticulously, are long; each one clocked in at around two to three hours playtime for me, since I played to avoid any detection at all.  Presumably you can play on if you're found out, but I never did, and I can't imagine it would be worth it.  If someone sees you and sounds the alarm, all sorts of new guards (previously absent on the map) come rushing out of buildings to swarm the area, everyone instantly knows where you are, and everyone starts shooting.  It's a mess, and short of hardcore speedrunning by a player deeply familiar with the maps, I can't imagine a scenario where an aggressive strategy would ever work in your favor.

Each level comes with nine goals to achieve to encourage replay; some are even mutually exclusive.  But frankly, I don't see myself ever going after the ones I missed.  I enjoyed plenty of the game, but the 35 hours I played were tedious enough that I'm in no hurry to repeat them anytime soon.  That said, though, Shadow Tactics is an excellent game, and well worth the purchase for anyone interested.  I got my copy on sale for 14 USD, and I consider it money well spent.  Even the full price of 40 USD can probably be justified - from a dollar per hour perspective, you should still come out on top.  Though it has its faults, I absolutely recommend this game.

It's real-time, but not so real-time as to be stressful. It's strategic, but in a puzzle-way versus a tactical-mastermind way. It openly encourages you to save-scum your way through the campaign, and so all guilt for doing so is gone. The puzzles for success will make you think a bit and do some trial-and-error, but not frustrate you or send you to YouTube to find a walkthrough. Perfect balance to make me feel smart without hurting my brain. Charming characters, rewarding levels and challenges. I found this game to be engaging and chill at the same time. Totally worth it.

The story of the game itself is actually quite clichéd.
You can basically guess what’s going to happen next.
But the way it subtly shapes the characters’ personalities
and portrays all kinds of interactions between team members
gives it a uniquely Eastern sense of melancholy and fate.
Everyone has their own past and story,
and everyone has their own preferred dynamic with others.
The whole experience is deeply immersive.
The difficulty of the game is subjective.
Personally, I found it pretty tough.
I spent 2 hours on the tutorial level,
and each subsequent level took me about 3 hours to clear.
Maybe I’m just bad at it, Orz.
Once you get used to the mechanics, though,
teasing the NPCs is incredibly fun.
You all have to try it.

I’m extremely looking forward to the sequel.

tl;dr: GOTY 2016.

I saw the screenshots, thought it looked like Commando's, so I downloaded the demo. An hour later I bought the game.

The game is a tactical stealth game set in Japan. You control 2 to 5 character and your missions consists of assissinating characters, stealing documents, listentening in on conversations to get info, freeing yourself from prison, etc.

The 5 characters each have their own personality and their own abilities. There is a ninja who has a shuriken so he can kill enemies from a distance and who can throw a rock to distract enemies. A samurai who can kill groups of enemies and is the only person who can kill other samurais in 1 on 1 combat. He is the strongest and can pick up 2 dead or unconcious enemies at once. A thief who can lure enemies with her whistle and then kill them using a trap. She is the weakest and can slowly drag enemies. A spy who can disguise herself, talk to enemies to distract them and who has a powder that reduces enemy field of view for a few seconds. And last there is a sniper, who has a pet which can distract enemies. You will need all of their abilities to beat the levels. Cool feature is that you can cue up 1 ability of each character and then execute them all at the same time. E.g. Talk to a group of enemies with your spy, while 2 other characters sneak up from behind. Cue up attacks with all 3 characters. Press enter and watch how your 3 characters kill the 3 enemies at the same time. The abilities are limited. For example you only get 1 shuriken. You have to pick up your shuriken after you kill an enemy. Your sniper only receives a few bullets. He will have to pick up bullets from containers. However, these are limited too. So you cannot just kill everyone with your sniper.

Enemies have view cones. These consists of 2 parts. A bright green, where the enemy will always spot you, and a dark green, where the enemy will only spot you if you are standing. Your characters can crouch and then crawl through these areas without being seen.

There are several enemy types. A simple guard who is easily lured from his location. A strawhat (guy with gun) who will not leave his post. Samurais, who cannot be killed 1v1, except by your samurai. A few levels in the game your characters receive guns, which temporarely cripple samurais, so your other characters can kill them too. Watch out though, they can still see you. So either run around their view cones, or use 2 characters; 1 to shoot, the other 2 kill. And there are civilians, who will run to enemies if they spot you. Some enemies will talk to other enemies while they are doing their rounds. Kill one of them and the other will wonder what's taking him so long to come back and will come looking for the other.

The level design is excellent and it feels like a real puzzle trying to figure out who you can kill without being spotted. Do I wait for guard to leave, or distract them, or do I go looking for a guard who is out of everyones field of view? There are bushes you can hide in. Bushes and obstacles reduce enemy field of view and some block enemy view completely. There is even a 3rd dimension. Your characters can climb onto buildings (some only using ladders and some can also use vines). Once on top of buildings your characters are usually out of view if they remain croushed. The most fun is that you can attack enemies from above. Then there are snow levels. The snow temporarely reveal your tracks. Enemies will spot these and follow them. Some levels are set during the night. Enemies see a lot less in the night due to the darkness, except around light sources. Some levels have water. Walking through water makes a sound and enemies can hear that. Your characters can interact with certain parts of the levels. E.g. cranes with boxes. Click on the crane and the box will fall, or plants in pots which can fall from balconies, etc.

The levels have replayability, because you can use different tactics to beat them. After you have beaten a level you can receive badges, which add to the challange. For example some badges can only be gained if you do not use a certain character, or if you do not kill anyone, etc.

The graphics are pretty good. Just look at the screenshots. Music is excellent. Story is a bit cliche.

This is my personal GOTY of 2016. I really enjoyed playing it. Cannot wait for the next game.

I recommend using the japanese voices (with subs), which are awesome. Is it a commandos clone? yes, but a damn good one!

This review was long overdue. Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun (will just refer to as Shadow Tactics) is a return to a genre I considered pretty much dead. This is a real time tactics game that for those that actually remember functions in the manner old Commandos or Desperados games did. While there are some RTT games around. They are usually done with modern progressions, RPG system and such. Example that comes to mind is singleplayer campaign of Dawn of War 2. Anyway this is the old RTT stealth based experience, but better. Soo much better.

Anyway for those who don't know how this works. Game is structured into missions. In each mission you control a fixed number of characters. Each character is unique (will go over that in a bit). The control is done in real time. Each mission will have objectives. Your goal is to accomplish the objective while traversing the level full of hostile enemies. Game focuses on stealth so you will try to sneak about, assassinate, hide bodies and so forth as you plot your way through the map and do objectives.

Now onto what makes this game so incredible. One this is essentially a puzzle game. A mass murder puzzle game at times (though you can get away with not killing anyone save for mission specific targets) but still a puzzle game. You will look at the map and you will see enemy positions, observe their patrols, unique features of the area and best assess how you can proceed. One guard may be in view of another guard, who may be in view of two other guards, who might be in route of a patrol, which may have something else come up. There are generally lots of moving parts and it requires both intelligent application of your character abilities and quick input of who does what and when. 

To illustrate the beauty of this game is to understand what you can do. The amount of input you have and amount of tools to observe and tackle your problems is phenomenal. You can turn the camera, unfortunately you can't change the angle at which you view, but turning it around is more than sufficient.  You can observe the view cones of anyone in the map. You can setup a marker to see which enemy at any given point can view that spot on the map. All your characters, their abilities have hotkeys. You need to quickly throw a rock. You press two buttons and then just press with mouse where you want it.  The game also has 'shadow mode'. Where you can queue up actions for your characters. Meaning you can tell a character to do something, and they will then do it on a button press. This lets you set up scenarios where you simultaneously perform many actions at once. Something that would have been impossible otherwise. You can also trigger each action separately (each character will have a key bind for that) or you can trigger all/remaining at once. It doesn't tale much imagination to understand how this expands the complexity of what you can do.

The game sets down rules of the world. You know exactly where an enemy can see, you know exactly how loud your actions will be. You know exactly what your interaction with anything will be at any given time. Enemies have view cones that are in two tones. Full, closer to enemy is where they will detect anything. Shaded is where they cannot detect stealth, meaning your characters that sneak, do stealth actions and such, but they CAN detect if you stand, run or try to do questionable actions. While they can't detect bodies on the ground in that portion, they can detect the act of body getting in that state. This create a massive layer for tactical applications. Then you have stuff like footprints you can leave in some surfaces (like snow), or loud surfaces like puddles that alert enemies. At night the full cone of vision is significantly less but any light source automatically makes them have a full view of that area. All this can be used for tactical applications. Manipulate AI that will follow footprints, leave a body by the torch so when patrol comes they will detect it from far away and come running. 

On top of all this there are your units. Each unit has multiple abilities and certain passive things they can do or are restricted to. All of them can for example sneak, but not all of them can swim, or climb vines or use hooks. All of them have some sort of stealth skill that can be used to alter an enemy's state. Make them look another way, lure them towards a sound, lure them towards a point, briefly restrict their cone of vision and much more. Each character has different time it takes them to kill, so for example Hayato who can kill an enemy in 1.2s is quite suited for stealth takedown. While Yuki takes almost triple that to kill someone. She makes up for it in other ways. While Hayato can only carry bodies while standing, he is faster than Yuki or Aiko who can slowly drag on the ground, but because they drag the body they won't be detected in the shaded view cone, while Hayato will. There are many such small subtle distinctions that make each character unique and interesting when applying solutions to many of the game's problems.

The game is complex, all of its systems are open ended and yet they all interact and work so incredibly well together. Think of it this way. If you think up some crazy plan, chances are it will work. You will know right away if its impossible, because you know what each action can do, but you will be amazed how much you can do when you combine them. Even after playing this, and after playing the newer released Desperados 3 I don't think I even scratched the surface on how much you simply can do in these games. They are a stealth masterpiece in just how much freedom you are given to solve your problems. Sure some of them will seem quite difficult, but more often than not, there are simple and clever solutions for it. 

Some of it will require fast and precise input, some of it will be just plain smart, make you go "wow that worked".  Game is challenging but so satisfying. It's the puzzle type of challenge that rewards both good execution, pattern recognition and weaving a thread through what seems impossible.

Game is divided into 13 missions. Each mission will have fixed characters. So each time your tactics will be different, not just because the map, objective and conditions are different, but because the combination of characters at your disposal force you to think differently than you may have been in the last mission. This is simply outstanding. Rarely you will have all five characters at your disposal, and no character is present in every mission. On top of this each mission has a set of challenges you can do. They give you restrictions how to complete the mission. Such as not killing anyone, or completing the map under a certain time, or not using Aiko's disguise. Some of these are quite difficult but add to replayability.

Story is set in feudal Japan. It is a bit cliche. You classic tale of Japanese warlords, betrayal, revenge and overly exaggerated sense of idiotic honor. Still even if the main story is nothing special, the execution of it is quite good. The way you weave the narrative as you essentially play it is fantastic. This isn't a story told through cutscenes. You are the one who will be doing the big plot points. The minimal stuff in between missions is just setup. You will feel the narrative unfold as you sneak by, shank people or throw boulders at them. I also love that the game has a great Japanese voice cast. I preferred it over the English one. 

If you are a person who likes tactical games, who likes stealth games. Shadow Tactics again is I daresay better than the old RTT games. It's systems are so incredibly well crafted, they work so well together. The possibilities of how you can solve the many of the game's problems are incredible. This game is a breath of fresh air and I loved it. Mimimi pretty much revived a dead genre with such authority, that I haven't seen such a thing in game development...well ever.

It took me 50 hours to fully complete the game, including all badges (side objectives) and achievements. This requires playthroughs on Hardcore and on a time limit for each mission; it will be relevant later. Based on both my Normal and Hardcore playthroughs, I recommend [i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i].

The game encourages you to first explore on your own by hiding badges and future missions until you play through each mission. I averaged around 1.5 hours on my first playthrough of each mission on Normal difficulty. That means that there's about 20 hours of gameplay if you don't care about completing all achievements.

I really enjoyed how every aspect of combat flows together. You can one- or two-shot all enemies, but the mission gets harder if another enemy raises the alarm. So you distract them with your characters' skills or use the environment like snow, darkness, and noise. You can plan these distractions by checking for patrols and lines of sight since there's no fog of war, or queue up an action on each character with "Shadow Mode." Watching your characters execute multiple enemies at the same time is always fun.

However, there's no slow motion or pause mechanic, except when time briefly slows down when your character is in an enemy's line of sight. When enemies are searching for you, they also move more randomly and are harder to predict or plan for. Quick save (F5) and quick load (F8) are your friends. Here's the catch: quick load remembers your total time played, which messes with the time limit for badges. You can restart the map and load to bypass this problem, but it's unintuitive and wastes your time.

Every map has a distinct design, multiple solutions, and Easter eggs. I enjoyed my time in this playground of murder and stealth. Once I finished my first blind playthrough of a mission on Normal, I watched speedruns on YouTube and followed them to finish my timed playthrough on Hardcore. I'd recommend watching, in no particular order, 4hinzo, Optibum, and panzerrunner.

The playable characters are distinct in skill set and character design... and I had nothing else nice to say about them until after a major plot twist. The consequences of the twist, not the twist itself, made me care so much more about the characters. The voice actors constantly use [i]-chan[/i] and [i]hai[/i] and Japanese proper nouns, but some of them are better at pronouncing these words than others.

Nevertheless, the story has a satisfying ending. I thoroughly enjoyed this game from start to finish. I bought the Anniversary bundle for $13.55 on sale, but I recommend the base game on its own merits.

[i]I'm still missing some achievements but the Steam Awards are here and [b]Shadow Tactics[/b] deserves a prize.[/i]

[b]Briefly: [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a real-time stealth tactics game, a true tribute to [i]Commandos[/i] games. Instead of soldiers, it's about ninjas and scheming in feudal Japan. And it fits the concept perfectly.[/b]

It's always a bit daunting to write about a game you love. [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] has everything you loved about [i]Commandos[/i] games, coming with a modern interface. It's also a great example that [i]Unity[/i] can create truly great games.

[h1]Long live Shogun[/h1]

The story puts you in the boots and kimonos of ninjas, samurai and other loyal servants of the Shogun. Story had me laughing and sometimes even crying - it has twists, prison breaks, betrayals, and assassinations.

Each character of the protagonist quintet has their unique skills and capabilities: e.g.
[list]
[*]ninja Hayato can throw shurikens and fool soldiers
[*]samurai Mugen can duel other samurai and carry heavy stuff
[*]street urchin Yuki builds traps
[*]geisha Aiko can put on a disguise that fools common soldiers
[*]Probably the strangest of the bunch is Takuma, an old gunsmith/sniper with a devious but cute pet raccoon Kuma.
[/list]
Level design is diverse: from battlegrounds to camps to fortified castles, every level is unique and many have unique gimmicks, like carts used for hiding or snow or water puddles that betray your position. No inside levels exist, though.

Different character skills and varied level design allows multiple possible approaches for each level. And after beating a level, one gets badges for completing them in different styles, like e.g. not killing anybody or not raising an alarm.

Combined with secrets scattered across the levels, this allows for hours of replayability for each level.

[h1]Enemies of Shogun[/h1]

Enemies have a cone-of-sight that fills when they notice a player, a body or other suspicious thing. The noticing speed can be adjusted by difficulty settings. On sight they shoot, and if you run out of health for any of the characters, they die and it's game over & reload/restart level.

AI is pretty good: enemy soldiers will go check why their pals haven't returned to their post, they follow your footsteps in the snow, check bushes, and call for help when they see you.

There are four types of AI characters:
[list]
[*]peasants, who either ignore the ninjas or go find guards
[*]common soldiers
[*]strawhats that ignore most distractions
[*]and the armoured, arrogant samurai
[/list]
It's amusing to watch the interaction of the samurai and common folk: after seeing a ninja, the peasants would run screaming for help and the samurai would just ignore them as "insolent peasants".

[h1]Team Ninja[/h1]

The characters have dialogue only in the cutscenes but they are generally well-made. There's both English and Japanese voice-acting. Personally, I opted for the Japanese one and found it splendid.

In the mission, characters are controlled with an RTS-like fashion: click a spot and the character will move there, perhaps do something there (kill, climb, operate machines etc.). Click and drag lets you choose several characters at once. Actions are limited by characters' abilities: e.g. samurai and oldman cannot use hooks to climb, while only the samurai can carry and throw boulders.

Since it's real-time, it's difficult to do really complicated maneuvers. This is alleviated a bit by the planning feature, which lets every character to execute their planned maneuver at the same time. This requires good timing to use properly, but pulling it off is ever so satisfying.

Sometimes the characters would get stuck in the vegetation or another character, therefore e.g. not killing them and resulting in an alarm or mission failure. Thankfully, it's possible to learn to avoid this.

[h1]Content and conclusions[/h1]

My first playthrough of all thirteen (13) missions lasted some 25-30 hours, IIRC. Altogether I've played almost 100 hours replaying missions for those elusive secrets and badges and still expect to put a few tens of hours more into it.

I'd like to congratulate [i]Mimimi Productions[/i]: not often am I so glued to my monitor for weeks as with [i]Shadow Tactics[/i]. I would love to see more of this!

A 2016 re-imagining of the 1998 classic [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commandos_(series)#Commandos:_Behind_Enemy_Lines]Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines.[/url] That may have its roots as far back as 1987 with Microprose's [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airborne_Ranger]Airborne Ranger.[/url] 

If you're familiar with neither, think [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndicate_(video_game)]Syndicate[/url]or for the younger gamer, [url=http://store.steampowered.com/app/268870/]Satellite Reign[/url], but with more stealth action, katana and shuriken, rather than guns and lasers, or cyberpunks. 

Shadow Tactics is a stealth-oriented real-time tactics game, set in feudal Japan.

The game is a retro top down-isometric. The sales experience is retro too. Preview at your lesiure, and for an unlimited time period beyond 2 hours, with a playable demo. No excess hype or early access nonsense where you pay to QA. None of that [i]release first and patch later[/i] approach. It works out of the box on day one. How things should be.

General presentation is lovely. A non-linear approach to completing each level, simple and intuitive UI optmised for K&B, stylised art and five engaging characters you can care about with unique and complementary abilities. All fully voiced in Japanese with English subs. Short cut scenes between levels fill out the back story.

It won't take long to complete. 20 hours to 40 hours maybe? But that's fine. Each mission has a unique and different tactical and visual feel; assuming the stealth genre always brings elements of [i]take out the enemy one by one without getting seen[/i] to complete each objective. A limited number of levels keeps it all fresh.

This game is FUN! It's just like [i]Commandos[/i] in the old days, except everything is very nicely put together - there are no glitches and no "pixel hunting", meaning you can focus entirely on strategy rather than wrestling with controls or the game engine. Even "casual" strategy players will enjoy this title, as the difficulty isn't daunting, yet there is still plenty of challenge to be had, even for seasoned veterans of the genre. 

GRAPHICS. No clutter, just intricately detailed (and pretty) textures and models. What I really appreciate is the sheer amount of artwork made for this game. Everything looks great - from the main menu to the finest character animations and cut scenes. As rich as the environments are, nothing is confusing or over-the-top. 

INTERFACE. Goes hand-in-hand with graphics. Highlights make it very clear what you can do, scripted events and dialogues guide you through the massive levels, tips and tutorials are always just a click away. Vision cones are very similar to other games of the genre, but there are some clever improvements here. The initial loading time for a level is a bit long, but once you see how intricate each level is and how fast the quicksave and quickload times are, you will understand. :)

SOUND. You can seamlessly switch between Japanese and English voice over and they're both done very tastefully. The sounds and noises are varied enough as not to get annoying. I love the way your characters talk to each other, or murmur their own monologues under their breath.

GAMEPLAY. This is the real question. And I must say, [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] did a great job. There are no overwhelming levels or strange difficulty fluctuations; game is moderately challenging throughout. Each level feels like a real, several-hours-long mission and I've enjoyed them all - various combinations of characters and environments always make you try new strategies. There is no obvious "cheese" strategy to beat all the levels (like shooting behind a corner in [i]Commandos[/i] and killing everyone that comes with your infinite-ammo-pistol) and you will genuinely have to think to beat most levels.

REPLAY? For me, definitely. Hidden achievements (revealed at the end of each level) are a good incentive to repeat levels and they often highlight a path you hadn't previously thought of. Not to mention the huge variability that comes from each character's skills.

If you like games like this, if you're a fan of the genre or anything stealth-like, or if you just wanna support great developers who weren't afraid to release a massive gameplay demo for free in 2016, you should probably buy this.

So... Shadow Tactics is a good game, well-put-together, as long as you know what to expect. Don't expect a squad-based tactics game, and don't expect a stealth game, either. Expect a puzzle game, played out with multiple pieces, with stealth mechanics as a veneer to cover the puzzles.

Also, expect a game designed to take advantage of quicksave/quickload. This is a game where you often need to make several things happen at once in a sequence of perfect timing, but there's no way to pause the game to issue commands or plan out your moves. You are expected to have to retry the same puzzle several times until you can get the timing just right. 

Unfortunately, getting to that point involves quite a bit of waiting, and that waiting drags on even longer if you're not making liberal use of the quicksave button. This is a game where you might spend several minutes getting from point A to point B, just to spend another ten minutes trying to get the timing perfect, and now you've managed to complete one small part of the larger puzzle. Most of these levels take over an hour to complete, despite the fact that you could run across them inside of 30 seconds. 

I really wanted to like this, but it takes all of the negatives of stealth games (lots of waiting, high consequences for failure, often hidden enemies), multiplies them by adding in the difficulties of planning and execution in real-time and with multiple characters, and doesn't give you the control that usually is a necessity in either the action or squad-based tactics games. As a result, the game often feels frustrating to me and I feel like it's wasting my time.

It’s rare to find a game that excels in the pillars of mechanics, storytelling, and art as consistently as Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. It has its share of blemishes, most prominent of which being camera controls that made me want to flip an entire hibachi table. But its needle-sharp stealth systems, cast of memorable characters with diverse abilities and personalities, and an uncommonly grounded saga set in a stylized feudal Japan left me with a sense of true accomplishment and a role in a well-told story.

Each of Shadow Tactics’ five characters has a particular set of skills that make them suited to different sneaky deeds, like hunkering down in bushes, isolating and executing enemies, and hiding the evidence before anyone notices. There were clearly times that called for Mugen, a samurai who can take out a cluster of enemies in a katana flurry, and times when it was a job for Yuki, a young thief who can lure solo enemies into traps. Other times, using them both in tandem allowed me to achieve what neither could alone, which created some great “Eureka!” moments.

It is difficult to believe that it'd take more than a decade for someone to tap into the sure-to-succeed genre of tactical RTS, in the style of Commandos. But nevertheless ST:BotS gives that experience with every possible bonus on top.

The game looks pretty gorgeous overall. The details, the terrain and the implementation of architecture is a smooth blend. What's more is that, under different circumstances, the game adds new behaviours. Snowy settings add the footsteps to consider (as enemies detect and follow them), while night-time missions change the entire high-viz / low-viz line of sight.

General premise is pretty simple. There is a decent (but not mind-blowing) storyline, unfolding each character and teaches the basic abilities and tactics. The gameplay is not noticeably different than Commandos or Desparados, but it's somehow simpler. Each character has five abilities, first three of which are specific to each, while the fourth and fifth are common items like pistols and first aid kits.

Characters vary in their styles and this plays a huge role in the gameplay overall, due to the challenge system implemented in the game. There are certain ways and means you can complete the game and doing things the hard way are rewarded (not using an tactic easily to pull off, or not using a character at all, or simply finishing the level in 10-15 minutes, et cetera). Furthermore, since none of these challenges are visible in your first playthrough, it automatically gives a motive for a replay.

The game consists of five characters: Hayato, a ninja with shuriken-tossing and distraction; Mugen, a samurai with the only viable 1v1 killing abilities; Yuki, an orphan girl with traps and lures; Aiko, another ninja but with disguises and blinding to boot; and Takuma, an elderly mechanic with a sniper rifle and a pet for distraction. There is an underlying narrative to bind them into the game and their voice acting is actually quite decent. 

As I mentioned, mechanics are pretty familiar but there're a few decent "quality of life" improvements. For instance, the game totes about three slots for quicksaves, which is a lifesaver for compulsive savers who accidentally overwrite previous games. The game also notifies you about saving your game with a green timer bar at the top that turns first yellow and then red to remind you. Lastly, the gameplay features a "Shadow Mode" - this enables you pre-designate any given action to a character and bind it a key. You can trigger each of them separately or let them loose simultaneously. This allows for precision interceptions at crucial timings or even outright clearing of zones by gunning down entire 3-5 strong patrols. 

The length of the game is quite adequate. More than dozen missions, with each taking about 2-3 hours (if you're particularly meticulous), not to mention the replaying for challenge objectives, it easily covers a couple of weeks. It's slightly high priced, but if offers a lot in return. 

My only disappointment is that the story was a bit lackluster - especially after figuring out the plot at less than halfway through the game, it was not a plot-twisting thrill-ride *but* everything else about Shadow Tactics truly carries the game off to a clean 9/10.

Great picture, nice storytelling, amazing gameplay, overall feels polished. Rare strategy/tactics that works well with gamepad. Commandos, Desperados, Robin Hood RTT genre gets reborn. I have not played any Commandos or Desperados game, so this genre or type of game is very new to me. This is an amazing game that everyone who likes stealth should play. Even folks who don't really like stealth should give this a go. What makes this game great?

1.) The characters are pretty nice. Sure they may be caricatures, but they're definitely not flat characters. 

2.) Get ready to save-scum. The game acknowledges this and makes saving and reloading very very quick.

3.) The gameplay is just amazing. At the beginning of every mission, you'll look at the entire map and think "this is hopeless, how will I ever do this without consulting a guide?" (to that end I HIGHLY recommend NOT to look at walkthroughs online. You will ruin the game experience). However, the magic of this game is that you can break down your overall mission into smaller, achievable steps. Kill dude X with a handful of guards surrounding him? Too hard. The game looks impossible, but is very much doable with a bit of patience and save-scumming. It's normal to finish 1 mission in 1-2 hours, and have a save/reload number of about 50 or so. 

The best part is shadow mode, when you can queue up actions of your different characters and execute them simultaneously, or even one at a time! Me, a guy who sucks terribly at strategy games, was able to pull that off??" Amazeballs.

I highly highly recommend this game.

RTS Stealth games are a rare breed, and this game is probably unlike most in the stealth genre in that you command a whole party with unique skill sets. The individual characters are fairly pedestrian—a traditional ninja that relies on mid-range shuriken and misdirection, a warrior with an emphasis on combat but weak stealth, a low mobility sniper, a trap master, and a disguise character that can move in-and-out of enemy lines undetected. That being said, the game stands out by giving players access to all of them (with your roster shifting from mission-to-mission), and treating each character as a set of interesting tools to solve your mission objectives.

Unfortunately, Shadow Tactics is also at war with its camera and has some frustrating design elements that sour the overall experience: 

1) Shadow Tactics is the type of games that demands absolute precision and timing from its players, but you only have limited control over the camera and some actions are only possible from specific camera angles. It's the absolute worst when you're about to execute a daring manuever or take out a guard, but you realize at the last second that you have the wrong camera angle and less than a second to find the correct one before a guard raises the alarm. I have no issue with stealth games being challenging, but it ruins the whole experience when you have to reload for the umpteenth time because terrible camera controls rather than a misplay. 

2) Shadow Tactics is horrid at communicating basic information to players. The basic game play loop revolving around abusing gaps in guard patrols and vision cones, but vision cones indicated in subtle shades of green that often blur into the surrounding color palette. If you are color blind, have vision problems of any kind, or even just use the wrong type of lighting around your computer monitor, players risk missing out on key information and be forced to reload for the umpteenth time.

3) Most importantly, Shadow Tactics is a game built around quick save abuse. The margin of error in Shadow Tactics is functionally non-existent, so players are encouraged to quick save frequently and reload whenever they make a mistake. In small doses, this is a lovely feature, but reloading dozens or even hundreds of times per mission will be common for most players (at least on their first playthroughs). After awhile, the game starts to feel less like a set of an exciting infiltrations, assassinations, and heists, and more like filling forms in triplicate after you reload for the umpteenth time because the camera bugged out at the last moment (and god help you if you haven't quick saved recently). 

I wanted to like Shadow Tactics. I really did. Still, that isn't an excuse for the critical lack of polish and terrible design decisions. If you can look past all of its awkward game mechanics, the camera that seems set up to fail, and tweak the graphics to avoid missing out on key information, you'll have a wonderful time with this rare gem. However, I can't recommend this game in good conscience to anyone but the most diehard stealth fans that can overlook its many, many flaws.

This is pretty much Commandos but in a more interesting setting, better story and characters. You form a small squad of specialists working for the Shogun to restore peace in the region. The characters are somewhat stereotypical, but in this game it's mostly a strength since you pretty much know what a character can do just from the archetype. The Samuraij is the most powerfull warrior, the ninja is agile and good at silent takedowns, the geisha, can disguie herself to create distractions. It's pretty much the same skills you had in Commandos. If you played those games, you will have a much easier time, and you will probably need it. The game is hard if you don't know what you are doing and understand the mechanics of the game. Mostly because there is no way to pause the action and issue commands and then unpause like in many tactical RPGs. But it's never unfair. If you fail it's always your own fault, and there is always an alternate solution to a problem. If you constantly fail, try something new. 

The characters are balanced, an all have their uses. For example the ninja and the samuraij can carry bodies faster, but the thief and the geisha are less visible when they move them (and the old sharpshooter can't move bodies at all). All the skills are varied and all have their own uses and work slightly different. The ninja can make enemies look in a different direction by throwing rocks, the thief can lure them from their post or patroll route and so on and the samuraij have a bottle of sake that guards will go and pick up (because all the guards are apperently drunks that go pick up discarded bottles of booze) and the sharpshooter have a adorable pet tanuki that he can send out that distract guards. The game will be much easier when you know how different skills work, it's still not a easy game (and I can't for the life of me understand how you are suposed to do the speedruns on some of the levels) but you will be much less frustrated if you know how each character work.  

There are some minor issues, it's more things that could be improved for a sequal rather than actual problems. 
Sometimes the game doesn't really understand where you are trying to click, especially in regards to different heights on the map and since the camera also only rotates in 90 degrees intervalls, this makes it somewhat cumbersome sometimes to correctly move around. A free rotating camera would be very nice to have. 

The system where you can set up an action for each character and then simultaniously execute them, is great but rather limited. For example, have the rifleman shot a samuraij, and then have the ninja preform a backstab to finish him of while the geisha throws a blinding bomb on a guard so he cant' see whats happening is awesome when you manage to pull it off, but it would be great if you could key more actions together or set up waypoints to time it better.  

Finaly, a multiplayer function would be great but that would probably throw the difficulty balance off somewhat, since you could have one player controling each character, making coordinating actions much easier.

After years of war, the Shogun unified Japan and established peace. When a mysterious warlord known as Kage-Sama emerges, jeopardizing the country's stability, Oshiro Mugen, a loyal Samurai, is assigned to reveal Kage-Samas identity and eliminate him and his allies.  
 
Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, is an isometric, real-time tactic stealth game, inspired by the Commandos and Desperados games. Take control of a small team to carry out various acts of espionage, sabotage, and assassination. Infiltrate heavily guarded fortresses, eliminate enemies, capture special targets, steal important documents, eavesdrop on conversations to collect information, or rescue other characters. In order to reach your targets, missions generally require you to methodically take out enemies, using distractions, lures, traps, and backstabbing to kill without raising the alarm. Take care to hide slain guards to prevent being discovered.  
 
During the game you recruit five agents specialized in infiltration and assassination to protect the shogun and the country's fragile peace. Each hero has its own set of skills.  
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2452538646 
Hayato is a grim ninja, never questioning tasks. He uses the typical weapons of a shadow warrior, shuriken and ninjato. Hayato is able to masterfully distract his enemies to kill them unnoticed in an ambush.  
 
Mugen is an honorable Samurai who is loyal to his Shogun with heart and soul. He leads the team and is able to kill more than one enemy at the same time. Mugen always carries a bottle of sake which he cleverly positions to lure guards into doom.  
 
Aiko is the transformation expert of the team. Disguised as a Geisha with an appealing appearance or as an unremarkable priestess, she can distract every enemy and arrange for her team to accomplish mission's unseen. 
 
Takuma, with his years-long experience as a sniper and gunsmith, supports the team as an expert at explosives and ranged attacks. After losing his leg in the war, he can’t fight actively anymore but this limitation does not make him less dangerous. With his rifle he is able to clear the way for your team from afar.  
 
Yuki is a clever, inquisitive young outcast. As an orphan, she grew up on the streets. Equipped with her bird whistle, she’s able to lure enemy guards into her self-built trap and into certain death.  
 
Character design is one of the highlights of the game. You quickly feel attached to the five heroes whose individuality is perfectly portrayed by very good voice acting, not only in cut scenes but throughout missions. Especially Yuki, the orphan, teenage, street-child, who's always ready for the kill, will be remembered as one of the most remarkable characters in computer games.  
 
If we take a look at the statistics there's something weird about Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. The overall Steam rating is 96% positive, which is outstanding. At the same time, most of my friends only played the game for less than three hours or only have it in their library without having played it ever. According to Steam statistics, only 10.5 % of all players collected the achievement that marks the end of the game, which means that most players did not finish the game. And there's a reason for this. 'Shadow Tactics' is a difficult game.  
 
The difficulty in this game gradually raises. Every mission is harder than the last. And while I struggled with early mission, thinking I'm never going to make it, endurance kept me going. The amazing thing is that re-playing earlier missions after completing the game felt easy. So, there's a learning curve. Don't give up. The game is totally worth it! Promise!  
 
The secret to success in 'Shadow Tactics' is coordinated attacks. When you start playing 'Shadow Tactics' you naturally select a single character to move forward and take out enemies. This however makes the game far more difficult than moving forward as a group and taking out enemies coordinated.  
 
The game offers the possibility to plan individual character actions and then carry them out all at once. This so-called shadow mode is highly effective to take out groups of enemies, that otherwise are very hard to overcome. Shadow mode lets you sweep away groups of enemies in swift, decisive moves. It’s a thrill to hit the button and see your minions move in tandem.  
 
Among hundreds of games there are only a few masterpieces. Shadow Tactics is definitely one of them, simply because the game gets all details right. Graphics, story, characters, music, controls, gameplay, AI, level design, it's all great! 
 
If you have a weak spot for tactical stealth games this one is not to be missed.

Before you bomb the forums with your complaints about the base price at launch please read this.

It's not just the game you are paying for. You are paying for a time machine that will take you to an era of game development in which the released games were bug-free at launch, in which there were free demos to try out and in which tactical real time strategy was a popular genre. 

The pricing scheme was also different back then. Nowadays you figure out what the market is ready to pay either through pre-order or crowd funding. Then you make the game with the funds you received and release it once the money are spent. The result is a game in which the devs made cuts and compromises on some crucial aspects of the game such as graphics and artwork (just decrease the texture resolution and call it retro), level design (use algorithms to automatically generate level and call it procedural), or game play design (just make it overall hard and call it rogue or just don't introduce any game play and call it sandbox), proper testing (release it with bugs and expect the mods to fix these, call it AAA) or without sufficient content (make and release the content once the sales from the launched product hit in, call it DLC).

Mimimi, the developer of Shadow Tactics did something different. They developed and released a finished product. They then calculated their development costs, made their sales projections and based on these they calculated the price of single copy of the game, such that the projected sales cover their costs and perhaps create some profit. If the base launch price is too high for you, wait for a sale or wait a couple of months until the price drops. In the meantime you can play the demo or (re)play its genre ancestors Commandos or Desperados. If you like the genre, consider buying this game at the full price - make it a success and show all game devs that we want more of these "time machines".

In short, this the most intellectually stimulating game in the "tactics" genre I've ever experienced. A true thinking (wo)man's pastime.

First off, the game is-real time and there is no pause button, other than opening the options menu. However, the characters you control can be easily hidden out of enemy sight by crouching in bushes, behind barrels, etc. Because the enemies follow strict patrolling paths or just stand still, this means that you can easily leave the game un-paused, go eat dinner for half an hour, and come back to nothing having happened. It essentially plays like it were turn-based. This lack of pressure allows the player to relax and spend luxurious amounts of time simply staring at the screen, thinking of how to solve the problem before them.

Most of the time the problem is "how do I move my characters from point A to point B without being spotted?". You view the map from a top-down isometric perspective and the camera can be freely moved, rotated, and zoomed to observe the entire map. Furthermore, there is no fog-of-war or any other such visual obstacles. All of this means that right from the moment the mission starts you know exactly: where the enemies are, where they are looking, and what paths are available to you to avoid danger, making planning ahead easy.

There are 13 missions to beat, each set on a unique map with zero random variables; your characters' starting positions and abilities, enemy behaviour, where the mission targets are, etc. are all predetermined. The developers have thoughtfully put all these pieces together in such a way as to create only a few viable paths through the level, and it is finding those correct paths amongst the plethora of false-hope ones that makes this game so intensely satisfying to play. When after 4 hours of trying I finally beat mission 12 without killing any enemies I felt like I had just ran a marathon - drained and (mentally) exhausted, yet very proud of being able to stand up the challenge.

The missions are tied together by an interesting story, told through cutscenes between each level and dialogue amongst your characters during gameplay. Whilst it isn't Mass-Effect-quality, the story is sufficiently deep and the characters interesting enough to draw you in and want to know what is going to happen next. The English version character voices are pleasant to listen to and you will quickly find yourself rooting for your merry band of protagonists.

One of the most wonderful attributes of this game are its unlimited quicksaves and quickloads - unusual features for a tactics game. Because of them I've never lost more than a couple dozen seconds to a mis-click or not noticing an enemy blending into the background. This has a surprisingly powerful effect on how enjoyable playing the game is, as you are spending all of your time on solving new problems, rather than having to mindlessly repeat sections of the game that you've already beaten (possibly more than once) just to get to back to where you were. It makes the whole experience a lot less frustrating, especially at the hardcore difficulty level.

And if all of that hasn't convinced you, the soundtrack is great, the graphics are pretty, there are lots of cool achievements to collect, and there are no scummy microtransactions / paid DLCs besides the soundtrack (which you should totally buy). A true hidden gem of a game.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Gorgeous graphics and art design. Every level looks beautiful, the animations are great, Being an isometric game, it looks amazing while not being very taxing at all and runs flawlessly. 
[*]Everything with regards to sound is great. Weapon sounds are awesome, the music is great and fits the atmosphere of the game, and the Japanese voice acting is phenomenal. Can't speak for the English VA.
[*]Gameplay is interesting and fun, and there's tons of depth. Levels are designed in a very open ended manner, with many different approaches available depending on your playstyle, as well as 9 optional challenges for each mission.
[*]Story is really cool, and the characters are great, both in gameplay and in the story. They have tons of personality, and each one has their own unique abilities and are useful in different ways. 
[*]A lot of replayability, with 9 challenges per mission, which are impossible to get in a single playthrough, and multiple paths through levels.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]I'd have liked to see a few more abilities in the game to add some variety, as each character essentially has an attack, some form of distraction, and some sort of indirect attack method or AOE attack. I'd have liked to see the more mobile characters possibly have some sort of escape ability, like a smoke bomb or something of that nature, or more varied non-lethal options. 
[*]The games Shadow Mode mechanic could use a way to set a timed stagger to when characters perform their actions, it would make it smoother and more flexible. 
[/list]

[h1]Neutral:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The game is hard. Normal difficulty is a serious challenge, and you'll likely quick save and reload many, many times on a first playthrough. I'm sort of slow and bad, so you may have a bit of an easier time, or a harder one. 
[*]The optional challenges are even harder, often to the point of being video game masochist only territory. I personally love that they are willing to throw out that extra challenge for people, but if you're a completionist, prepare to pull your hair out on some of these.
[*]Despite being a reasonably long, sort of party based game, there are no RPG mechanics or character skill progression elements to speak of. You do get new characters over the first few missions, and get a new item as well, but that's it, there's no real upgrades or progression beyond that. Some people look for that in any game they play, and it wouldn't necessarily be unsuitable here, each level is designed with a particular set of abilities in mind, and as you progress through the game you learn new applications of each characters abilities and ways they can work together. This is going to largely be down to preference. 
[/list]

Just a few quick thoughts. The gameplay and replayability value are well worth the money. The campaign took me about 30 hours on first playthrough and I already know I'll be definitely returning to grab some of those challenging badges.

The game's difficulty seems to be raising with each following level, and as you think you've figured it all out, it throws something at you that stops you in your tracks. For long enough to keep you invested, but not long enough to really frustrate you.

Shadow Tactics is by far the most difficult stealth game I've ever managed to finish. While Blades of the Shogun isn't for everyone, it is an expertly crafted experience that combines adept storytelling with complex yet easy to control stealth gameplay. I would highly recommend this for anyone who enjoys stealth games but, because of the nature of the genre, it is hard to recommend to newcomers because of the steep difficulty curve and its dependence on quicksaving/quickloading.

It's hard to talk about the story without spoilers because it's only 13 missions long (and I don't know anything about Japanese history) but it at least feels more grounded in reality here than most stealth games. There are no magic spells, no ninjutsu scrolls, no ridiculous acrobatics to fly around the map. Your characters are believable human beings and while yes, two of them are actual ninjas, they just move more gracefully than other humans in their world. The only tools at your disposal that really require suspension of disbelief are actually the old sniper's gear. While the plot becomes predictable after the halfway mark, it is still motivating to watch it unfold even if your characters are going through constant suffering and strife.

For hardcore fans, each mission has 9 badges for bonus objectives: 3 are mission-wide primary objectives (like not entering water or not using a specific character's skills), and 6 are secondary objectives that involve some mutual exclusion. This means even with perfect gameplay it will take multiple playthroughs for perfectly clearing a mission. Initially the gameplay can feel constrictive, as if there's only one way to play through each mission, but as your skills improve your strategy will widen and each map feels like a playground... Well, for most missions. Some of the latter missions had me ragequitting from the lack of cover and every enemy having 2 people watching him. The last mission also breaks away from the play style of the rest of the game and feels impossible without sneaking through long distances with one character at a time. Overall, the campaign is well crafted and enjoyable but certain missions I'm okay with never playing again (at least not without a walkthrough).

The game is clearly designed for savescumming; if you don't want to be  quicksaving and quickloading every minute or so, this isn't the game for you. Apart from that, Shadow Tactics is a beautifully crafted and well paced stealth game that only comes along every few years. There are positives, like the pretty environments and lively art direction, but because of a combination of frustrating elements, the game becomes a frustrating grind that discourages tactical thinking and has you fighting the controls and save scumming constantly.

The maps are large, and the missions typically take an hour or two to beat, but there's no way to see the whole map at once. The zoom is woefully limited, meaning that planning a route through from the start to the goal is impossible. You find yourself taking on every little area one at a time, unable to plan for what's next, and looking back and realizing it would have been faster to go another way. Every guard is watched by at least one other guard. Killing guards becomes a process of tediously killing your way through an entire section of the map just so you can kill one guard that was blocking a gate.

For a stealth tactics game, the maps are also shockingly linear. Sure, it's open, but there's only one path that doesn't lead to certain death. After a time, you get the impression that every map has one main designed path with a few shortcuts, and every area, every section of the map is just a puzzle to solve (and time correctly). I didn't once feel like I could experiment with using different combinations of abilities, or one mission, going vertical, or going sneaking on another. I can't count the number of times I thought "Oh, I'd have loved to have this character right now, I wonder how I could use his explosive with her powder.." etc. except that every mission has a specific loadout of characters. I never felt like I had a creative choice in my use of abilities or characters. And even with the characters you get, working together is pointless. Even the abilities each character has seems unnecessarily limited. Only one character can throw rocks? Only one character can make a luring noise? It's arbitrary decisions like this that make the gameplay uncreative.

The squad mechanics are almost non-existent. I found myself playing most of the maps one character at a time, only changing when I faced a situation that required a different character's abilities. You can only control one character at a time, except to move, and even then it's a disaster because they all have different movement speeds and collide with each other constantly, frequently catching the guards' attention. The only way to use your characters together is using "shadow mode" which allows you to queue actions from different characters so you can execute them at once. HOWEVER, shadow mode only allows you to queue up ONE ACTION per character, making complex planning (i.e. shadow TACTICS) virtually excluded by design. The game wants you to control characters and make decisions in real-time, but making real-time decisions is impossible because the maps are crawling with guards, and this is [i] not a combat game. [/i] If you're spotted by a guard, game over is all but certain. Reinforcements begin to shoot from afar, you cannot fight more than one guard, you cannot run, you cannot become invisible. Even if you do manage to escape, the entire map will be on alert, making the rest of the mission nearly impossible. And your other characters CANNOT HELP AT ALL because again, REAL TIME. If you're spotted, your sniper can't take out the guard, your heavy can't clear the guards, because without that action-planning, by the time you switch to them, it's too late. The game becomes about timing, waiting and save-scumming over and over to get characters across the map, one by one.

That brings me to the save-scumming. It's included in the gameplay by design, even going as far as to include a timer reminding you to constantly save. Some others don't mind this, but I personally found it frustrating and flow-breaking. The game relies on save-scumming because it's the only way the player can time moves perfectly enough to succeed because the stealth, squad teamwork, and combat mechanics are not effective enough alone because they can't be properly planned and executed. It makes the gameplay tedious, and when it collides with the controls, it becomes truly frustrating.

The majority of the game relies on the mouse, and a few clunky hotkeys. Switching between characters takes too long to perform actions across characters in real-time. Executing actions, however, is the true nail in the coffin. I can't count the number of times I've clicked on a guard to kill them, and instead, without my realizing, the kill skill wasn't toggled, and my character walks right up to the guard and sits there, waiting for death. Me too, buddy. Or that I thought I clicked on the ground but instead clicked on a wall, and then my character walks out in front of a guard, reload the save. Or, that I had the wrong character selected, and again, ruined the play. The camera is not suitable for the amount of tight spaces and vertical elements in the game. You can't look top down, and rotating the camera requires stopping whatever else you're doing.

All these elements combine to make the gameplay an absolute grind that discourages tactical gameplay in favor of save-scumming over and over to solve precision timing situations.
